# FairFahren multiplayer race — conventions and harnesses

## When to Use

Use when working on the multiplayer/race implementation in the FairFahren repo
(`docs/plans/g-multiplayer/`, phases per `02-implementation-phases.md`), or any
touchpoint of `server/raceState.js`, `server/protocol.js`, `src/net/*`, or the
smoke tooling (`tools/smokeClient.mjs`). AGENTS.md owns the standing gates
(npm run check, review agent, size budget); this skill carries the parts those
gate bullets don't say.

## Procedure per phase

1. Read the phase's Deliverables + Tests sections and map each test name to the
   brief's acceptance line it satisfies — the test list IS the spec; write the
   test names before the module. Zero-dependency and pure-data rules from
   AGENTS.md apply; don't re-litigate them.
2. Adding/altering a message type: extend the `MESSAGES` registry in
   `server/protocol.js` FIRST (fields + validators — one shared encode/decode
   pair is driven by it), then run `node tools/protocol-table.mjs` and swap the
   table into NOTES.md between the markers. A unit test asserts the embedded
   table equals the generated one; skipping the regen fails check.
3. Keep side-effect ownership by injection: raceState gets `now/send/close/
   schedule`; src/net modules take every time source as an argument. Nothing in
   `server/` or `src/net/` may call `setTimeout` itself except `server/main.mjs`
   (the real-socket shell) — that is what makes the whole state machine testable
   on FakeNet's virtual clock.
4. Implement module + tests together (repo says speed over TDD ceremony), then
   `npm run check` BEFORE ending the phase: suite must not regress and the size
   budget must still pass (`src/net/*` COUNTS toward the client budget;
   `server/` does not).
5. End of phase: run the real-socket smoke (recipes in the reference), update
   NOTES.md (protocol table, decisions, how-to-test section), then run the
   review agent as AGENTS.md requires. Fix findings with a live repro first —
   see pitfalls.
6. Never commit or push unless asked; leave solo mode untouched — every phase
   must keep `npm start` behaving exactly as before the race work existed.

## Pitfalls

- **Callback slots are ASSIGNMENTS, not calls.** WsConnection/FakeConnection
  style APIs expose `conn.onMessage`/`conn.onClose` as settable properties:
  never write `conn.onClose(fn)` (calls a null slot; crashes the server on the
  first disconnect), and when a wrapper installs its own handler, wrap-and-void
  the existing one instead of overwriting it, or you get a ReferenceError (the
  wrapper's closure cannot see the caller's locals).
- **Close-reject order.** A race-state reject (`close(conn, 4000, ...)`) fires
  during `connect()`, before any client-side handler exists — capture reject
  codes in the test world's injected `close` wrapper array, not via onClose.
- **Joins race the start button.** Connect all fake/real clients in parallel and
  the early `start` (roster >= 2) closes the stragglers with 4001 mid-lobby —
  stagger joins (or start only when the roster is full) whenever a test/smoke
  wants everyone racing.
- **Relayed positions carry the SENDER's id.** When relaying `pos`, take the
  id from the sender's player record, not the receiver you are looping over —
  an easy variable-shadowing bug the receiver-side asserts will catch.
- **Finish reports accept `racing` OR `finished`.** Racers still on the road after
  the first finisher must be able to report (settle happens later); the guard is
  stage in {racing, finished} + once per player + no DNF flag. Accepting only in
  `racing` breaks the second finisher's report whenever the first flips stage early.
- **A new server→client type needs its client dispatch in the SAME change.**
  Adding a message to `server/protocol.js` without adding the handler case +
  `on.<event>` callback in `src/net/client.js` makes decode() accept it while the
  client drops it silently — the live feedback never fires and nothing throws.
- **Turn-away codes need re-delivery in tests.** A reject captured in the injected
  `close` wrapper must be re-delivered with its code by the test's client onClose
  handler — the peer side of a close is codeless, and a bare no-arg close maps to
  client stage 'dropped', so the 4000/4001 'turnedAway' states stay unreachable
  through FakeNet otherwise.
- **Rematch (`again`) wipes per-player state, including `gone`.** A racer whose
  connection died mid-race reappears on the rematch grid with a dead socket, and
  the fresh 30-s window settles them DNF again — that is the designed behavior;
  don't 'fix' the reappearance, and never reuse old-race finish data (seed bumps
  +1; finish/dnf/pen/gone all cleared).
- **Interp buffer contract.** push() ignores snapshots with t ≤ newest (never
  teleports backwards); sample() clamps at the newest snapshot — no extrapolation
  — and takes shortest-arc headings. Testing unordered input or extrapolated
  motion means testing the wrong contract.
- **Real WebSocket refuses send() before open.** createNetClient sends the join
  in its constructor; on a real socket that first call throws
  InvalidStateError and the page dies silently. The browser wrapper (main.js)
  must queue outgoing frames until 'open' and flush them then — FakeNet masks
  this because it queues itself.
- **Background tabs never run rAF.** When driving the real browser via the
  harness, a "dead" loop with empty HUD spans is usually the page being
  background-throttled, not a bug: call Page.bringToFront (or use new_tab) and
  re-probe before debugging.
- **Protocol wire format is FLAT.** Messages travel as `{type, ...fields}` —
  test drivers and smoke tools read `m.players`, not `m.data.players` (decode()
  re-adds `.data` only on the receiving side of unit code).

## See also

- `references/testing-recipes.md` — the fakeNet world() harness and the
  real-socket spawn driver for multi-player smoke runs.

messages.content:
Verified on your machine just now: the server booted on port 8077, two script clients joined, and both got `countdown → go`. Here's the whole thing, plain-English.

## The 3 different ways to test it (easiest → most "real")

### 1. `npm test` — logic only, no action
The race rules live in `server/raceState.js` as pure rules with no sockets, no timers of their own. Tests plug in a **FakeNet** — think of it as a toy walkie-talkie set plus a rewindable stopwatch, so you can say "advance 3 seconds" and see exactly what the referee would do — without any browser or real network. Run `npm test`, or `npm run check` (tests + size budget) as the full gate.

### 2. Real socket, no browser — script players
The server program is also the referee: `node server/main.mjs --seed 42 8077`. Then in a **second** terminal, spawn fake taxi drivers:

```bash
node tools/smokeClient.mjs Alice 8077   # each is one "player"
node tools/smokeClient.mjs Bob 8077
```

Each script client connects over a real WebSocket (same wire path the browser uses), says "I'm Alice", starts the race when 2 are in the lobby, drives a fake arc, reports a finish, and prints everything the server says. That's how I got the verified output above. To do it all in one shot (spawns the server + N clients as children, kills them after a hard time bound), there's a ready one-liner harness — ask and I'll drop it in `tools/`.

### 3. Real socket + real browsers — the actual game, twice
Same machine works fine; two tabs are two "players".

1. `node server/main.mjs --seed 42 8077` (any 807x port)
2. Open `http://localhost:8077/?online` in **two windows** (use one normal + one incognito so they don't get mixed up)
3. In each: type a name → Join. The lobby shows who's there; when 2+ are in, the Start button unlocks — click it in one window
4. You'll both see the countdown, then the ampel (traffic light) goes green at the same instant for everyone, and you drive. Since both windows read the same seed, they're racing on the identical city

## Gotchas that will bite you

- **Never use port 8080 for probes** — that's the `npm start` dev/static server. Pick 8070–8079. A server that finds its port taken exits with code 1 and *no message*: check the port with `netstat -ano | grep 8077` and kill strays with `taskkill /F /PID <pid>`.
- **Joins race the Start button.** If one client joins a second late, the early starter's race can kick the latecomer out with close-code 4001 mid-lobby. Spaced joins (~300 ms apart, like I did) or "start only when everyone's in" fixes it — in tests the turn-away only shows in the server-side reject log, not the client's close event.
- **Background tabs freeze.** A tab you're not looking at stops rendering (rAF throttling), so its "player" looks dead — click into the window before hunts.
- **Solo is sacred:** `npm start` must behave exactly like before all this existed — no sockets, no lobby. Never route solo through the net path.
- One client crash or disconnect at any point → server marks them DNF after the window; that's designed, not a bug.

Want me to save the one-shot spawn driver as a permanent `tools/smokeRace.mjs` so test #2 becomes `node tools/smokeRace.mjs 3`?
and on different machines?

Good news: the server is already built for this — line 66 of `server/main.mjs` binds to `0.0.0.0`, which means "listen on every network card, not just a single machine/localhost". Your Wi-Fi IP right now is **10.0.11.30**.

## The recipe (server machine = yours, players on other laptops)

**On your machine (the host):**
1. Start the server the same way: `node server/main.mjs --seed 42 8077`
2. Tell Windows to let strangers in — the first run will pop the firewall prompt ("Node.js wants network access"); allow it for **Private networks**. Or add an explicit rule yourself:
   ```
   netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="FairFahren race" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=8077
   ```
   (I checked — no such rule exists on your machine yet, and I didn't create one. That command only adds a rule when you run it.)
3. Find your IP if it ever changes: `ipconfig` → look at the Wi-Fi adapter's "IPv4 Address".

**On every other machine (players):**
1. Open a browser and go to your *own* machine's game
2. Enter `http://10.0.11.30:8077/?online` (host IP + port + `?online`)
3. Name → Join → someone clicks Start. Same race as if you were in a second tab.

The only real difference from the single-machine test: `localhost` is replaced with the host's IP. Everything else — lobby, seed, countdown, ampel — is identical, because it's the same one server deciding the rules.

## Two things to know

- **Why `?online` matters:** a player landing on `http://10.0.11.30:8077/` without it just gets the solo game running on *their* machine — they'd drive alone and wonder why nobody sees them. The `?online` flag is what opens the lobby.
- **Timing across machines:** each browser syncs to the host's server clock over the wire, so the green light goes off at the same instant for everyone, latitude of ping permitting. On Wi-Fi with big lag, expect remote taxis to wobble slightly — the other drivers are reconstructed from position snapshots.

## Testing it without a second laptop (the honest test loop)

- `tools/smokeClient.mjs` is hard-coded to `ws://localhost:8077/ws`, so a script "player" can't join from another machine. To fake a remote player on the host, that's fine for the wire path — but for the *LAN* path specifically, the realistic check is: start the server, run `curl -I http://10.0.11.30:8077` **from the host first** (proves the server answers on the LAN address, not just localhost), then have the second machine open the browser URL.
- Keep the same discipline as before: port 807x only, and if it doesn't work, the two usual suspects are (a) the firewall prompt was declined, or (b) the two machines aren't actually on the same network (guest Wi-Fi often isolates devices).

Want me to add the firewall rule (I'd need to run that `netsh` command), and/or a small branch in `tools/smokeClient.mjs` so it takes `ws://<host>:<port>` instead of hard-coding localhost — handy for scripted players joining from another machine?
